cards.title: Generation model evaluation overview
questions: what is the generation model evaluation page
what is the rule-bound generation screen

what is the rule-bound generation on one gpu study
short summary of the skyrule generator model screen

what did the seven configuration screen conclude
cards.answer: It's an October 2026 case study where I screened seven local model configurations, covering six models, on the real generator behind my personal project Skyrule. The generator writes a plan, then a piece, and code checks both. Its yield had stalled at 3 of 20 groups. Under a decision rule frozen before the run, Qwen3.8 27B accepted 7 of 20, and a second pre-registered round on 60 new groups replicated it, 24 against 11. The public IFEval ranking disagreed with the task ranking. Qwen3.8 is eligible for the release route, not adopted, and nothing on the page is release validation.

cards.answer: A trial run on 20 frozen test groups finished within its bounds but kept only 3 of 20, against a pre-registered bar of 9. A separate measurement found every first plan failed at least one check, with a median of five failing checks per plan. The anchor words were present for all 20 groups, but one rule banned the phrase "each other" while every accepted wording of one goal contained it. So the low yield could come from the model, the serving setup, the instructions, or all three. The screen asked one narrower question: with prompt, checks and bar fixed, does another local configuration accept clearly more groups?

cards.title: The decision rule and what clearly more means
questions: what was the screening rule in the generation model evaluation
what does clearly more mean in the model screen
how many more accepted groups earned a full trial

how did she decide which model earned a full trial

what does earning a full trial mean for a local model
what is the screening threshold for the generation screen
cards.answer: An arm earned a full trial if it accepted at least four more groups than the baseline and did not accept fewer on the first try. I wrote that before any model loaded and froze it by hash. I'm clear about its limits: the four-group margin is a screening threshold with no calibrated false-positive control across several candidates, and with seven arms on 20 groups one arm can clear it by luck. That's why passing only earned a full trial, not adoption. Fluent writing that fails a check counts as a rejected piece, so the generator's own checks were the score.

cards.answer: Seven main configurations covering six models. A was Qwen3-32B on vLLM with AWQ, the current generator and the baseline. B was the same model on Ollama with Q4_K_M. Then Qwen3.8 27B, GPT-OSS 20B with thinking set to low, Nemotron 3 Nano, Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B, all on Ollama. Each arm is a bundle of model, server, quantization, chat template and default sampling, and the results describe those bundles. An optional eighth arm, Qwen3.8 27B with thinking low, hit its per-arm time cap and was not compared.

cards.answer: Before any model loaded I froze the screening rule by hash. The fidelity gate said the baseline must reproduce the trial run's 3 of 20 within two groups, or nothing is concluded. It accepted 3 of 20, so the gate passed, though that only establishes fidelity under the pre-registered gate. The bench's records show each copied file's hash checked against the release version. The design went through two independent model-review rounds, the bench had 67 CPU tests, and a later independent audit of the write-up found overstatements, now corrected on the page.

cards.title: Running the real generator and GPU fit
questions: did the screen use the real skyrule generator code

cards.answer: Each arm ran the release generator's own code, prompt, retry budget, seed and checks on the same 20 frozen groups, pointed at a different model. Every Ollama arm had to load 100% onto the GPU at a 16,384-token context or be refused, and all six did. The vLLM baseline ran on its own server, so its fit wasn't checked the same way. The bench held a lock on the card, checked ownership before destructive steps, and stopped an arm if it saw a model it hadn't loaded. Rejected and timed-out groups stayed in the denominator of 20.

cards.answer: Only Qwen3.8 27B met the rule: 7 of 20 accepted against the baseline's 3, with a Wilson interval of 0.18 to 0.57. First-try acceptance was 0 of 20 for both, so it didn't lose there. Paired by group, both accepted 2, only Qwen3.8 accepted 5, only the baseline 1, exact McNemar p = 0.22, unadjusted and descriptive. GPT-OSS 20B also got 3, Qwen 3.6 got 2, Qwen3-32B on Ollama got 1, and Nemotron 3 Nano and Gemma 4 each got 0. With 20 groups and one seed, small differences aren't resolved.

cards.answer: The same Qwen3-32B accepted 3 groups on vLLM with AWQ and 1 on Ollama with Q4_K_M. Total calls were about equal, 102 and 104, so per accepted group the Ollama arm used about three times as many, 104 against 34. Server, quantization and possibly template and sampling defaults changed together, so I can't say which one mattered. In this single run the two bundles differed. The screen doesn't show how reproducible that is or how much the server alone contributes, which is why I describe every result as a comparison of bundles.

cards.answer: Failures differed by stage. Gemma 4 had 3 groups rejected at the plan stage and 14 at the writing stage across 42 writing calls, and accepted none. The current Qwen3-32B configuration had 15 groups rejected at the plan stage. That suggests testing a different model for each stage, which I did in round 2. It doesn't establish which model plans or writes best on its own. It's a lead from failure analysis, and it needed its own pre-registered test before I'd treat it as anything more.

cards.answer: Per accepted group, Qwen3.8 27B used 16.4 calls and 2,733 output tokens against the baseline's 34.0 calls and 11,021, so about half the calls and about a quarter of the tokens in this run. In round 2 it was 14.8 calls and 3,194 tokens against 42.7 and 7,516 for the current prompt. These are success-normalized totals across all stages, not measured completion times. On a single card it matters, but full-library time also depends on batching, latency and how yield varies across other groups, so I don't claim a library time from them.

cards.title: Why Qwen3.8 differed from Qwen3-32B

cards.answer: The records show where they differed, not why. Qwen3.8 used 27 plan calls against 41, with 491 average output tokens per plan against 727, and 12 groups rejected at the plan stage against 15. At round 0 it failed DUP1 on 2 groups against 7, GOAL1 on 10 against 15, and LAUNDER2 and INTERACT2 on 0 against 4 each, but NEV1 on 9 against 0. Both had 15 groups fail BF8. Shorter plans coincided with fewer flags on some checks. The screen can't separate training, size, architecture, template, quantization or sampling, so the cause stays a hypothesis.

cards.title: The instruction contradiction in the prompt

cards.answer: One rule banned the phrase "each other" while every accepted wording of one goal contained it, so some failures may reflect incompatible instructions rather than either model. It surfaced when the prompts were reconstructed after a measurement showed every first plan failed a check. The aggregate BF8 counts don't say how much of the failure that conflict caused. I tested a candidate fix in round 2 as a separate factor, and its benefit wasn't shown at that precision: an average of 7.5 points, interval minus 3 to 18. The contradiction still needs its own repair and test.

questions: what was round 2 of the generation model evaluation

cards.answer: Yes, it held. In a second pre-registered round frozen before it ran, with a new seed and 60 new groups from one job, Qwen3.8 27B accepted 24 of 60 against the current configuration's 11, a difference of 21.7 points with a 95% Newcombe interval of 6.6 to 35.5. Paired, only Qwen3.8 accepted 18, only the current one 5, both 6, neither 31, exact McNemar p = 0.011, and first-try acceptance wasn't worse. Scope is narrow: one seed, one placement, one relation and one goal, and a bundle comparison. It supports a full release route, not release validation.

cards.title: Model versus prompt in the two by two
questions: did the prompt fix or the model matter more

cards.answer: The model mattered more than the prompt. Across the two-by-two, Qwen3.8 on Ollama against Qwen3-32B on vLLM averaged about 21 points, bootstrap interval 9 to 33. The candidate prompt contrast averaged 7.5 points, interval minus 3 to 18, so a prompt benefit wasn't demonstrated at this precision. Qwen3.8 accepted 24 of 60 with the current prompt and 28 with the candidate, and the baseline 11 and 16. The interaction estimate was minus 1.7 points, interval about minus 20 to 18: none detected, though meaningful interactions remain compatible with the data. These secondary estimates are exploratory.

cards.answer: It didn't demonstrate a benefit. Gemma 4's plans were accepted for 52 of 60 groups against 27 for Qwen3.8's own, but with Qwen3.8 writing from Gemma's plans, 25 groups were accepted against 24 with its own plans: an estimated gain of 1.7 points, interval minus 17 to plus 20. Holding Gemma's recorded plans fixed, Qwen3.8 writing accepted 35 points more groups than Gemma writing, interval 23 to 47. The staged arm used two passes, replaying Gemma's plan responses byte for byte, so the resource figures mix two models and aren't costs of a live pipeline.

cards.answer: IFEval has 541 prompts, and prompt-level strict accuracy is the headline. Gemma 4 31B scored 0.900, the baseline Qwen3-32B on vLLM 0.830, Qwen 3.6 0.823, Qwen3.8 0.806, Nemotron 0.793 and GPT-OSS 20B 0.725. Before use, the reference checker reproduced the paper's published GPT-4 results within two prompts and two instructions, not exactly. Paired against the baseline, Gemma passed 61 prompts it failed and failed 23 it passed, p below 0.0001. Qwen3-32B on Ollama was flagged contaminated in round 2, so it's descriptive only, 0.839, and not compared.

cards.title: Why the IFEval and task rankings disagreed
questions: why did gemma 4 top ifeval but fail the generator

cards.answer: The two rankings differed. Across the six configurations with clean IFEval results, Gemma 4 scored highest at 0.900 and accepted 0 of 20 and then 4 of 60 task groups, while Qwen3.8 scored below the current configuration, 0.806 against 0.830, and accepted the most. IFEval tests general verifiable instructions, and the generator's checks test this task's specific rules, so they measure different things. I use a public benchmark to build a shortlist, but here the task's checks and a rule written in advance decided what earned a full trial. Neither establishes writing quality.

cards.answer: One NVIDIA RTX 5090 with 32 GB, one request at a time, 20 fixed prompts. Qwen3.8 27B used 19,324 MiB after load at 122 tokens per second with 0.71 s to first token. Nemotron 3 Nano was fastest at 336 tokens a second, GPT-OSS 20B smallest at 13,156 MiB and 280 tokens a second, Gemma 4 31B 128 tokens a second at 23,560 MiB, and the vLLM baseline 68 at 30,436 MiB. These are single-stream rates on this card, not aggregate throughput or production capacity, since vLLM batches in real use. Licences reproduce Ollama's metadata, so check each model's own before use.

cards.answer: Incidents were recorded as they happened, and affected results were discarded or flagged. In the first IFEval window the bench's watcher saw an unexpected model load and stopped Gemma 4's run. I first attributed it to a morning check-in job; a later diagnosis traced it to an hourly agent round that falls back to a local model when the resident service is down. The next window started early at my request without removing that interference, and Nemotron's IFEval run was contaminated, probably from the same cause, though that wasn't measured. A text-encoding error then stopped the window before B and D. Round 2's first two windows were refused by an output-path guard, fixed in two lines. Task scores were unaffected.

cards.title: What the screen does not show
questions: what are the limits of the generation model evaluation

cards.answer: Several things. The checks are the score, not a measure of writing quality beyond what they test, and a model judge gave 0 scores. Twenty frozen groups and one seed say little about small differences or other groups, and round 2's 60 groups came from a single job. Each arm is a bundle of model, server, quantization, template and sampling, so I can't attribute a difference to any one of them. The best round 1 result, 7 of 20, was still below the bar of 9. Other task types weren't tested, and nothing here is release validation or a production decision.

cards.answer: Qwen3.8 is eligible for the release route, not adopted. Taking it into the generator is a release decision: its own canary run, an independent quality review and the project owner's approval of the model change. The next piece is a pre-registered fine-tuning experiment with its own build, which reserves the round 2 groups from training and validation data. Its first pilot stopped on a server setup error, recorded and fixed, and has been re-queued, so no fine-tuning result is reported. A wider model search remains possible later. This is level 2 research, so nothing on the page is release validation.

cards.answer: I did the evaluation design, the orchestration and the failure analysis. The workload belongs to Skyrule, my self-funded personal project, and the bench ran on one RTX 5090 using Ollama and vLLM. My coordinating agent, Claude, unloaded an unexpected model by hand in the first IFEval window so the restore and results could proceed. The design went through two independent model-review rounds, and an independent audit of the write-up found overstatements that are now corrected on the page. It is an October 2026 case study of screening evidence, not a production decision.

cards.title: Engineering lessons from the screen
questions: what were the takeaways of the generation model evaluation
what did she learn from the qwen3.8 screen
why measure the task as well as the leaderboard
why decide before you look in a model comparison
why have the write-up audited

why does a shared gpu need isolation
what lessons came from comparing bundles
how did the pre-registered rule keep the screen from becoming adoption
what would she do differently in the generation screen
what is the main lesson of rule-bound generation on one gpu
cards.answer: Six things. Measure the task as well as the leaderboard, because the IFEval ranking and the task ranking differed. Check the harness and the instructions, since a reproduced baseline doesn't prove the prompts are sound and a review found a contradiction. Compare bundles and say so. Decide before you look, and keep the decision small, so a screening result doesn't become an adoption. A shared GPU needs isolation, not good timing. And have the write-up audited: the first draft had causal claims the data didn't support, a units error and figures from the wrong window. The corrected page says less and is more defensible.

cards.title: Why the method is set up this way
questions: why use the generator's own checks as the score

cards.answer: I held the prompt, checks and bar fixed so any change in accepted groups could be attributed to the configuration, and I used the generator's own code checks as the score so there's no model judge and no scoring subjectivity: 0 scores came from a model. Rejected and timed-out groups stay in the denominator of 20, so a configuration can't look good by dropping hard cases. The screening rule was frozen by hash before running, on 20 frozen groups. Only counts and check names are reported, never generated text. In round 2 I tested the candidate prompt as a separate factor rather than changing it under the screen.
